Recovery-Directed Symbolic Distillation
of Neural Likelihoods

Kianté Fernandez ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Department of Psychology Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles Affiliation: Los Angeles, CA 90095, USA Email: kiante@ucla.edu    Xinwei Li Affiliation: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering Affiliation: National University of Singapore Affiliation: Singapore Email: xinwei.li@u.nus.edu
Abstract

Amortized neural likelihoods enable computationally expensive inference for models with analytically intractable or unspecified likelihoods, but their black-box nature limits interpretability. We introduce a symbolic distillation pipeline that converts trained neural likelihoods into explicit, interpretable expressions optimized for efficient parameter estimation. Our approach uses a recovery-directed objective to guide symbolic regression toward expressions that preserve parameter-recovery accuracy rather than merely approximating the likelihood function. Candidate expressions are evaluated on held-out datasets and selected using a criterion that jointly accounts for expression complexity, parameter-recovery performance, and distributional distance from the learned likelihood. We evaluate the pipeline on the diffusion decision model, a classical cognitive model, whose analytically tractable likelihood provides ground truth for controlled evaluation. The proposed recovery-directed objective improves parameter recovery over standard symbolic-regression objectives. The resulting symbolic likelihoods enable over 100 times faster parameter evaluation than both neural likelihoods and, when available, the exact likelihood, while maintaining a manageable loss in precision. We further demonstrate these computational benefits in Bayesian hierarchical inference on empirical data. Our pipeline provides a lightweight interface for integrating symbolic distillation with existing neural-likelihood estimation methods and can be adapted to a range of simulation-based inference settings.

1 Introduction

Cognitive science formalizes hypotheses about mental processes as mechanistic models (Kriegeskorte & Douglas, 2018). Such models specify an explicit generative process 𝓖⁡(𝜽,ϵ)\bm{\mathcal{G}}(\bm{\theta},\bm{\epsilon}) (ϵ\bm{\epsilon} for stochastic noise) for observed behavior 𝒚\bm{y}, encoding substantive hypotheses of underlying operations and indexed by a small set of interpretable parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta}. To further validate the hypotheses, the models are often fit to experimental data, which requires estimating the parameters from observed data, typically through the likelihood p⁡(𝒚|𝜽)p(\bm{y}|\bm{\theta}). However, many cognitive models with richer and more realistic assumptions fail to have a tractable likelihood.

One popular class of cognitive models, sequential sampling models (SSMs), demonstrates this tension. SSMs posit that decisions arise from the noisy accumulation of evidence over time until reaching a decision threshold (Ratcliff, 1978; Forstmann et al., 2016). Under a forced-choice task with options 𝒞\mathcal{C}, each observation 𝒚=(RT,c)\bm{y}=(\mathrm{RT},c) therefore comprises a response time RT\mathrm{RT} and a chosen option c∈𝒞c\in\mathcal{C}. SSMs are widely adopted across domains, including perceptual decision-making and clinical research (Ratcliff et al., 2016), value-based and consumer choices (Clithero, 2018; Krajbich et al., 2026, for reviews, see), and moral dilemmas (Maksimenko et al., 2025, e.g.,). Nonetheless, only the simplest case of SSMs is analytically tractable in likelihood p⁡(RT,c|𝜽)p(\mathrm{RT},c|\bm{\theta}), such as the Navarro–Fuss series (Navarro & Fuss, 2009) for the classic drift-diffusion model (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008, DDM,), whereas its scientifically interesting extensions (e.g., collapsing decision bounds and leaky accumulators) generally lack a closed-form likelihood.

Simulation-based inference (SBI) addresses the parameter estimation of cognitive models with infeasible likelihoods by using generative processes 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} (Cranmer et al., 2020a, a review,). The amortized variants (e.g., likelihood approximation networks (Fengler et al., 2021, LANs;), neural density estimators (Boelts et al., 2022), and amortized Bayesian workflows (Radev et al., 2020; Radev et al., 2023)) have become particularly popular, owing to their reusability across datasets. That is, a neural network is trained only once on simulated data and can then be applied to any new dataset at negligible cost, without further simulation or retraining. Moreover, toolboxes like HSSM (Fengler et al., 2026) for SSMs have integrated pretrained likelihood approximations pϕ​(𝒚|𝜽)p_{\bm{\phi}}(\bm{y}|\bm{\theta}) by amortized SBI into a standard probabilistic-programming interface. However, the learned likelihood pϕ​(𝒚|𝜽)p_{\bm{\phi}}(\bm{y}|\bm{\theta}) is a black box, because the network weights ϕ\bm{\phi} carry no substantive interpretation. Consequently, the recovery analysis, approximation diagnosis, and structural insight into the likelihood must all be done numerically.

Symbolic regression (SR) may offer a way to open this black box. SR is a recently growing supervised learning approach that discovers symbolic mathematical expressions ff from data {(𝒙,f0​(𝒙))}\left\{\big(\bm{x},f_{0}(\bm{x})\big)\right\} by searching the space of closed-form expressions ℱ\mathcal{F}, trading off accuracy against expression complexity (Makke & Chawla, 2024, a review,). The resulting analytic alternatives f∈ℱ∗f\in\mathcal{F}^{*} are not only inherently interpretable and auditable but also differentiable and cheap to calculate. Whatever the search technique, the canonical objective ℒ⁡(f,f0)\mathcal{L}(f,f_{0}) is to minimize the expected error between the candidate expression ff and the real value f0f_{0}. Although, from the perspective of SR, the probability density pp is simply another target function (i.e., f0​(𝒙)=log⁡p⁡(𝒚|𝜽)f_{0}(\bm{x})=\log p(\bm{y}|\bm{\theta}) and 𝒙=(𝜽,𝒚)\bm{x}=(\bm{\theta},\bm{y})), the standard objective ℒ\mathcal{L} is misaligned with the purpose of obtaining closed-form approximations for the implicit cognitive models, namely efficient and accurate parameter estimation with an interpretable structure.

In this work, we propose a pipeline that distills analytical expressions from neural approximations to make parameter estimation easier (Section 2). First, the neural likelihood pϕp_{\bm{\phi}} is admitted only after a sequence of SBI diagnostic checks. Then the symbolic regression search is guided by a recovery-directed loss function ℒλr​(f,log⁡pϕ)\mathcal{L}_{\lambda}^{r}(f,\log p_{\bm{\phi}}) (Section 2.2), which substantially improves parameter recovery over the standard symbolic-regression objective (Section 4.2). Finally, each candidate expression on the Pareto front ℱ∗\mathcal{F}^{*} is fit with a full Bayesian sampler and ranked by how well it recovers the parameters on held-out data. We evaluate it on the simplest DDM, whose exact likelihood permits direct assessment of approximation accuracy and helps identify the sources of estimation error. The resulting symbolic likelihoods are tens of times faster to evaluate than compiled exact and neural likelihoods at the size of one subject, and more than 100 times faster on large datasets, while maintaining a manageable loss in precision (Section 4.3).

2 Method

Figure 1 summarizes the pipeline, in which each stage consumes the output of the previous one. In Stage 1, a neural likelihood pϕ​(𝒚|𝜽)p_{\bm{\phi}}(\bm{y}|\bm{\theta}) is trained and checked. In Stage 2, symbolic regression under the recovery-directed loss ℒλr\mathcal{L}^{r}_{\lambda} produces candidate expressions ℱ∗\mathcal{F}^{*}. In Stages 3–4, each candidate is fit with the No-U-Turn Sampler (Hoffman & Gelman, 2014, NUTS;) in PyMC (Abril-Pla et al., 2023) and ranked by how well it recovers the parameters.

To set up, we place independent uniform priors 𝝅⁡(𝜽)\bm{\pi}(\bm{\theta}) on each parameter over its range Θ\Theta. All data are simulated from 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} in the group format {(𝜽(g),𝒚1:Km​a​x(g))}1:Ga​l​l\left\{(\bm{\theta}^{(g)},\bm{y}_{1:K_{max}}^{(g)})\right\}_{1:G_{all}}, in which each parameter set 𝜽(g)∼𝝅⁡(𝜽)\bm{\theta}^{(g)}\sim\bm{\pi}(\bm{\theta}) generates Km​a​x=1,000K_{max}=1{,}000 independent trials. Different stages use different groups, and the number of trials drawn from each group depends on the stage (Appendix C).

2.1 Stage 1: amortized SBI admitted by diagnostics

Simulator Specification.

DDM (Ratcliff, 1978; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008) describes the forced binary choice process, hence 𝒚=(RT,c)\bm{y}=(\mathrm{RT},c), where the choice outcome set 𝒞={−1,+1}\mathcal{C}=\{-1,+1\}. The DDM accumulates evidence at time τ\tau by

d​V​(τ)=v​d​τ+d​W​(τ),V⁡(0)=a⁡(2​z−1),dV(\tau)=v\,d\tau+dW(\tau),\qquad V(0)=a\,(2z-1), (1)

where the within drift noise W⁡(τ)W(\tau) is a Wiener process. The decision is determined when |V||V| hits a boundary at ±a\pm a. That is,

𝓖⁡(𝜽,ϵ)=(RT=t+inf{τ:|V⁡(τ)|≥a},c=2​𝟙​(V⁡(RT−t)>0)−1).\bm{\mathcal{G}}(\bm{\theta},\bm{\epsilon})=\Bigg(\mathrm{RT}=t+\inf\big\{\tau:|V(\tau)|\geq a\big\},c=2\mathbbm{1}\big(V(\mathrm{RT}-t)>0\big)-1\Bigg). (2)

𝜽=(v,a,z,t)\boldsymbol{\theta}=(v,a,z,t) contains drift rate vv, boundary half-separation aa, relative start point zz, and non-decision time tt. Notably, given the symmetric property of first passage time on both boundaries, the parameter θ\theta can be identified with single-side joint density (i.e., p⁡(RT,c=1|θ)p(\mathrm{RT},c=1|\theta)). For detailed settings, see Appendix H.

Amortized SBI Structure.

Because 𝒚=(RT,c)\bm{y}=(\mathrm{RT},c) combines a continuous and a discrete variable, the joint density factorizes exactly (Boelts et al., 2022) as

log⁡pϕ​(RT,c∣𝜽)=log⁡pϕflow​(RT∣𝜽,c)⏟normalizing flow+log⁡Pϕclass​(c∣𝜽)⏟classifier.\log p_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\mathrm{RT},c\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})\;=\;\underbrace{\log p_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\mathrm{flow}}}(\mathrm{RT}\mid\boldsymbol{\theta},c)}_{\text{normalizing flow}}\;+\;\underbrace{\log P_{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\mathrm{class}}}(c\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})}_{\text{classifier}}. (3)

We model the continuous part with a normalizing flow trained by conditional flow matching (Dinh et al., 2017; Papamakarios et al., 2021) and the discrete part with a small classifier (architectures in Appendix B). This module can be replaced by any amortized SBI method that allows likelihood evaluation, including methods not trained specifically for likelihood estimation, such as all-in-one SBI (Gloeckler et al., 2024).

Surrogate Diagnosis.

So that approximation errors do not propagate to later stages, the neural likelihood must pass a diagnostic gate on held-out validation data, which checks the calibration of the RT flow and the choice classifier and how well the parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} are recovered (Appendix B).

2.2 Stage 2: Symbolic distillation for log-density

SR freely searches the space ℱ\mathcal{F} of analytic expressions composed from a fixed operator set 𝒪\mathcal{O} and inputs 𝒙\bm{x}, returning a Pareto front ℱ∗⊂ℱ\mathcal{F}^{*}\subset\mathcal{F} of candidates that trade off accuracy against complexity. For density approximation from a previous neural surrogate, the input data is 𝒙i=(𝜽i,𝒚i)\bm{x}_{i}=(\bm{\theta}_{i},\bm{y}_{i}), while the output is the log neural likelihood log⁡pϕ​(RTi,c=1|𝜽i)∈ℝ\log p_{\phi}(\mathrm{RT}_{i},c{=}1|\bm{\theta}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}.

SR searching techniques.

We use PySR (Cranmer, 2023), which represents each candidate as an expression tree (𝒙\bm{x} as leaves and 𝒪\mathcal{O} as nodes) and evolves several populations in parallel by genetic programming. The operator set 𝒪\mathcal{O} includes binary operators {+,−,×,÷}\{+,-,\times,\div\} and unary operators {exp,log,⋅,(⋅)2}\{\exp,\log,\sqrt{\cdot}\,,(\cdot)^{2}\}. Runs are budgeted by the same time budget, and their Pareto fronts are unioned and de-duplicated on the printed form denoted by ℱ∗\mathcal{F}^{*}.

The recovery-directed objective ℒλr​(f,log⁡pϕ)\mathcal{L}^{r}_{\lambda}(f,\log p_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}).

Compared to the classic mean square error (MSE) loss function

ℒ⁡(f,log⁡pϕ)=1N​∑i(f⁡(𝒙𝒊)−log⁡pϕ​(yi|𝜽i))2,\mathcal{L}(f,\log p_{\boldsymbol{\phi}})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\left(f(\bm{x_{i}})-\log p_{\phi}(y_{i}|\bm{\theta}_{i})\right)^{2}, (4)

the recovery-directed objective ℒλr​(f,log⁡pϕ)\mathcal{L}^{r}_{\lambda}(f,\log p_{\bm{\phi}}) in Equation 5 adds two penalty terms, a recovery term 1−ℛ⁡(f)1-\mathcal{R}(f) weighted by the hyperparameter λ\lambda and a constraint term B⁡(f)B(f),

ℒλr​(f,log⁡pϕ)=1N​∑i(f⁡(𝒙𝒊)−log⁡pϕ​(yi|𝜽i))2⏟density fit+λ⁡(1−ℛ⁡(f))+ 103​B​(f),\mathcal{L}^{r}_{\lambda}(f,\log p_{\bm{\phi}})=\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{N}\textstyle\sum_{i}\bigl(f(\bm{x_{i}})-\log p_{\phi}(y_{i}|\bm{\theta}_{i})\bigr)^{2}}_{\text{density fit}}\;+\;\lambda\bigl(1-\mathcal{R}(f)\bigr)\;+\;10^{3}B(f), (5)

where the last term enforces two hard constraints, with B⁡(f)B(f) counting violations. First, every element of 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i} must appear in ff after simplification (e.g., (−h)+h=0(-h)+h=0 removes hh), since a parameter cannot be recovered from an expression that omits it. Second, ff may not contain constant leaves. Adding a constant to a log-likelihood does not change its estimates, so forbidding constants removes redundant expressions and the cost of optimizing them in PySR. Constant factors can still arise through simplification, as in h+h=2​hh+h=2h.

1−ℛ⁡(f)1-\mathcal{R}(f) stands for the approximated parameter recovery error given the grid recovery proxy on training data of the current candidate ff. The proxy θ~j(g)\tilde{\theta}_{j}^{(g)} for the parameter set θ(g)\theta^{(g)} on jt​hj_{th} element is derived in Equation 6 such that the summed log-likelihood under ff over KK training trials, ∑kf⁡(𝒚k(g),{θ−j(g),θ~j(g)})\sum_{k}f(\bm{y}_{k}^{(g)};\{\theta_{-j}^{(g)},\tilde{\theta}_{j}^{(g)}\}), achieves its maximum over all MM candidates grid {γj​m(g)}1:M\{\gamma_{jm}^{(g)}\}_{1:M} over θj\theta_{j}’s domain Θj\Theta_{j}.

mj​g⋆=argmaxm=1,⋯,M∑k=1Kf(RTk(g),c=1,{𝜽−j(g),θj=γj​m(g)}),θ~j(g)=γj​mj​g⋆(g)m^{\star}_{jg}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{m=1,\cdots,M}\sum_{k=1}^{K}f\left(\mathrm{RT}_{k}^{(g)},c=1,\{\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(g)}_{-j},\,\theta_{j}{=}\gamma_{jm}^{(g)}\}\right),\qquad\tilde{\theta}_{j}^{(g)}=\gamma_{jm^{\star}_{jg}}^{(g)} (6)

As a result, the recovery performance is valued by ℛ⁡(f)=1P​∑j=1P(ρ~j−e~j)\mathcal{R}(f)=\frac{1}{P}\sum_{j=1}^{P}\left(\tilde{\rho}_{j}-\tilde{e}_{j}\right), with ρ~j=corrg⁡(θ~j(g),θj(g))\tilde{\rho}_{j}=\operatorname{corr}_{g}(\tilde{\theta}_{j}^{(g)},\theta_{j}^{(g)}) and e~j\tilde{e}_{j} the fraction of groups whose argmax sits on a grid edge. For detailed PySR setting and hyper-parameter selection, please check Appendix A.

2.3 Stages 3-4: screen and validate

Screening criteria.

Each candidate expression f∈ℱ∗f\in\mathcal{F}^{*} is used as the likelihood to fit every subject in the scoring bank with NUTS (500500 warm-up and 500500 sampling iterations, 22 chains). For each parameter θj\theta_{j}, recovery is measured by the correlation rjr_{j} across subjects between the posterior mean θ^j(s)\hat{\theta}_{j}^{(s)} and the generating value θj(s)\theta_{j}^{(s)}. A parameter passes if rj>r0=0.5r_{j}>r_{0}=0.5 and fewer than half of its estimates lie within 1%1\% of the range from either bound, since estimates that pile up at a bound can still correlate with the truth. An expression passes if every parameter does. Convergence is monitored through the per-subject R^\widehat{R} and the number of divergent transitions, and the passing expressions, which already trade density fit against complexity on the Pareto front, are ranked by their weakest parameter recovery, minj⁡rj\min_{j}r_{j}.

Additional diagnostics.

Parameter recovery alone does not show that an expression describes individual subjects well. We therefore also checked the validated expressions with diagnostics that are standard in applied cognitive modeling (Schad et al., 2021; Gelman et al., 2020). In addition to the convergence checks above (R^\widehat{R} and divergent transitions), we ran posterior predictive checks and simulation-based calibration (Talts et al., 2018, SBC;). More specifically, the former metric compares choices and RTs simulated from each subject’s posterior with the observed data, while the latter tests whether the sampler and the compiled expression together return calibrated posteriors on data generated from the expression itself. Details and results are in Appendix F.

3 Related Work

Recent symbolic distillation frameworks treat SR as the final stage of a surrogate-modeling pipeline, distilling the input–output behavior of a trained neural network, or of its components, into closed-form expressions (Cranmer et al., 2020b; Tan et al., 2026). These frameworks target general input–output maps and impose no function-specific constraints before or during the search. Comparatively little work addresses probability densities specifically. Algorithms like MESSY (Tohme et al., 2024) guarantees a valid density by restricting the estimate to the maximum-entropy family, and Liu & Li (2026) recover closed-form probability mass functions for discrete variables. The closest continuous analogue of the surrogate-then-distill design, AI-Kolmogorov (Rajendram et al., 2026), distills a nonparametric kernel density estimate with PySR under the MSE loss of Equation 4, so its result inherits the surrogate’s error and does not depend on the model parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta}. Our method differs in two ways. It checks that the neural likelihood preserves the parameters before distillation, so the resulting expression is a function of 𝜽\bm{\theta} that can be used for inference, and it distills with an objective aimed at parameter recovery rather than density fit.

4 Results

4.1 Symbolic likelihoods recover the DDM parameters

We first asked whether the pipeline can produce a closed-form likelihood that recovers the parameters of the DDM. To answer this, we used 6060 simulated subjects with 10001000 trials each, none of whom were used to train the neural likelihood or to run the search (Appendix C). Recovery was measured for each parameter as the correlation across subjects between the true value and the posterior mean. As a reference, we fit these subjects with the exact analytical likelihood, which shows how well the parameters can be recovered from this amount of data when the likelihood is known exactly. As expected, recovery was nearly perfect (r=.98r=.98–1.001.00 for all four parameters; Figure 2a, top row).

We then asked whether information was lost when the analytical likelihood was replaced by the neural likelihood in Stage 1. It was not. The neural likelihood recovered the parameters as well as the analytical likelihood did (r=.98r=.98–1.001.00; Figure 2a, second row), and the two gave nearly the same estimate for each subject (r=.96r=.96–1.001.00; Figure 2b, middle row). Because the expressions are distilled from the neural likelihood, not the analytical one, any further loss in recovery can be attributed to the distillation step (Appendix B).

Finally, we fit the same subjects with a symbolic expression found under the recovery-directed objective (Equation 5, λ=1\lambda=1; third in Table 1). Recovery was lower than under the analytical likelihood but well above our criterion of r>.5r>.5 for every parameter (r=.85r=.85, .91.91, .88.88 and .98.98 for vv, aa, zz and tt; Figure 2a, bottom row). To check whether the fixed search budget (Appendix A) was enough to approximate the neural likelihood well, we compared the expression’s estimates with those of the neural likelihood. We found they agreed closely for each subject (r=.89r=.89–.98.98; Figure 2b, bottom row).

For comparison, the third row of Figure 2a shows an expression found under the standard MSE objective (Equation 4). Its correlations looked nearly as good (r=.89r=.89, .81.81, .78.78, .98.98), but it failed our criterion because its estimates piled up at the bounds of the parameter range, for aa in 53%53\% of subjects and for zz in 85%85\%. The correlations stayed high because whichever bound an estimate landed on still tracked the true value, which is why our criterion also rules out such estimates (Section 2.3).

In addition to recovering the parameters, the distilled expressions are short enough to read. We next asked how many expressions in the full pool met our criterion. The pool contained 33713371 expressions from 124124 independent searches run under five values of the recovery weight λ\lambda (Section 4.2), and 276276 of them recovered all four parameters. We ranked them by their weakest parameter, that is, by the lowest of their four correlations. Table 1 lists the top five, and all five are written out in Appendix G. Because the same 6060 subjects were used to rank the expressions, we also refit the top five on 9090 further subjects that were never used for any selection. All five still recovered every parameter (weakest r=.81r=.81 to .90.90; Table 1).

We highlight the second of these (Expression 2). Its weakest correlation is within .004.004 of the top-ranked expression, yet it is about half the size (2525 nodes against 4444), and it had the best posterior predictive fit of the five (KS=.130\mathrm{KS}=.130). The expression is given as follows:

f=1a​[a−(RT−t)​((a2​e−2​zRT−t−v)2+ez2)].f=\frac{1}{a}\left[\,a\;-\;(\mathrm{RT}-t)\left(\Bigl(\frac{a^{2}e^{-2z}}{\mathrm{RT}-t}-v\Bigr)^{2}+e^{z^{2}}\right)\right]. (7)

It recovered vv, aa, zz and tt at r=.94r=.94, .91.91, .88.88 and .97.97, with few estimates at the bounds (at most 10%10\% of subjects, for aa).

The expression is also easy to interpret. Writing τ=RT−t\tau=\mathrm{RT}-t for the decision time and D=a2​e−2​zD=a^{2}e^{-2z}, its main term is −τ(D/τ−v)2/a-\tau\,(D/\tau-v)^{2}/a. This has the same form as the exponent of the Wald density, −τ(d/τ−v)2/2-\tau\,(d/\tau-v)^{2}/2, which is the leading term of the exact DDM first-passage density at short decision times, with dd the distance from the start point to the boundary (Navarro & Fuss, 2009). In both, the term is largest when the drift rate vv equals d/τd/\tau, the rate at which evidence would have to accumulate to reach the boundary at exactly that time. The logarithm of that leading term, fit the same way, recovered the parameters about as well (weakest r=.86r=.86 on the held-out subjects, against .90.90 for Expression 2; Table 4), so the search found an expression as good as the known approximation without being given it. Posterior predictive checks and simulation-based calibration for this expression are reported in Appendix F and Section H.2.

4.2 The recovery-directed objective makes recovery possible

We next asked what allowed the search to find these expressions. Every expression discussed so far was found under a loss that included the recovery term. To isolate its effect, we compared searches that differed in the weight on that term, λ\lambda (Equation 5), holding other settings the same (Table 3). Without the recovery term (λ=0\lambda=0, which reduces to plain MSE), 3636 independent searches produced 968968 expressions, and only 1212 of them (1.2%1.2\%) recovered all four parameters. The drift rate and the start point were the main obstacles. Only 22.9%22.9\% of these expressions recovered vv, and only 6.9%6.9\% recovered zz. With the recovery term at λ=1\lambda=1, 9595 of 486486 expressions (19.5%19.5\%) recovered all four parameters, and the pass rates for vv and zz rose to 52.7%52.7\% and 25.1%25.1\% (Figure 3b–c). Averaged over searches rather than expressions, the rates were 1.5%1.5\% and 18.5%18.5\%, with non-overlapping 95%95\% intervals (Table 3). Notably, without the recovery term, no expression recovered zz better than r=.69r=.69 (among those whose estimates did not pile up at the bounds), whereas every set of searches that included it exceeded .85.85 (Figure 3a).

However, prioritizing recovery did not always help. Across the five values of λ\lambda, the proportion of expressions that recovered all four parameters rose from 1.2%1.2\% at λ=0\lambda=0 to 19.5%19.5\% at λ=1\lambda=1 and then fell to 2.1%2.1\% at λ=10\lambda=10 (Figure 3b). The best weight also differed by parameter. Recovery of tt fell from 99%99\% at λ=1\lambda=1 to 81%81\% at λ=10\lambda=10, whereas zz was recovered most often at λ=3\lambda=3 (30.6%30.6\%; Figure 3c).

4.3 Symbolic likelihoods are fast

We next asked how much the closed form saves in computation. We timed one summed log-likelihood for Expression 2, the analytical Navarro–Fuss series, a LAN (Fengler et al., 2021) and our neural likelihood, on datasets from 3030 to one million trials (Table 2; Figure 4). To make the comparison fair, the analytical series and the LAN were taken from HSSM and compiled, and each likelihood was timed alone and with the gradient that samplers like NUTS need at every step. At 10001000 trials, the size of one simulated subject in our tests, Expression 2 took 0.0100.010 ms, or 0.0150.015 ms with its gradient. This is 2727 to 3939 times faster than the compiled analytical series, 7070 to 8484 times faster than the LAN, and more than 100,000100{,}000 times faster than our neural likelihood, whose cost is dominated by integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE). The advantage grew with the size of the dataset. At one million trials, Expression 2 took 0.510.51 ms against 315315 ms for the compiled analytical series and 161161 ms for the LAN.

Expression 2 is fast because it needs neither a network nor a solver, nor an infinite series summed to a set precision. Every exponential in it depends only on the parameters, so the work for each trial is plain arithmetic. The price of this speed is the modest loss in recovery described in Section 4.1.

4.4 Application to empirical data

So far, recovery and speed were both measured on simulated data. We therefore asked whether the symbolic likelihoods also hold up on real data. We refit a published dataset (Cavanagh’s frontal-theta study; Cavanagh et al., 2011, 39883988 trials, 1414 participants) as a hierarchical DDM in which every parameter varies by participant and drift rate also depends on frontal theta, as in the original analysis (Appendix E). We fit this model once with HSSM’s compiled analytical likelihood and once with each of the 100100 best expressions, under identical priors and sampler settings. 9696 of the expressions converged (R^<1.01\widehat{R}<1.01).

At the level of individual participants, the expressions ordered participants in nearly the same way as the analytical likelihood on boundary separation aa (median rank correlation .97.97), drift rate vv (.93.93) and non-decision time tt (.90.90; Figure 5a). They ranked participants poorly on zz (.29.29), mainly because participants barely differ on zz in these data (analytical posterior means from .48.48 to .50.50), and even the neural likelihood agreed with the analytical ranking at only .72.72.

Crucially, the symbolic likelihoods were also faster on these data. In the full model, the converged expressions took a median of 7373 s against 174174 s for the analytical likelihood. To time a larger set of expressions, we also fit a simpler model in which only the drift rate varies by participant (Appendix E). Across 267267 expressions, the median fit took 1414 s against 386386 s, a 2727-fold speed-up, and fewer than 2%2\% were slower (Figure 5b). Both likelihoods needed about the same number of gradient evaluations, so the gain reflects the cheaper evaluation of each (Appendix E).

5 Limitations & Future Discussion

A number of limitations warrant consideration. First, the discovered expressions are estimating functions rather than normalized densities, so they define only a generalized posterior (Bissiri et al., 2016) whose intervals carry no calibration guarantee. Second, they estimate tt largely from the fastest responses, which makes them sensitive to fast guesses (Section H.2). Third, every result here concerns the DDM, a deliberate test case whose exact likelihood let us check every step. The approach matters most for models without a tractable likelihood, such as those with collapsing bounds, and applying the recovery-directed objective to such models is the most important next step. Finally, the search produces hundreds of expressions that recover the parameters. Interpreting them as a set, for example by removing terms one at a time, could reveal which structures carry recovery.

6 Conclusion

In this study, we proposed a pipeline that distills a neural likelihood into a closed-form expression and asked whether such an expression can recover the parameters of a cognitive model. Using the DDM as a proof of principle, we found that it can and that this depends in large part on incorporating the recovery-directed objective. The resulting expressions are fast to evaluate, and an application to real data showed that this speed advantage carries over to hierarchical fits.

More broadly, our results suggest that the flexibility of simulation-based inference and the transparency of closed-form likelihoods need not be traded against each other. By asking a symbolic search to preserve properties important to the application (parameter recovery), it may be possible to have both.

Reproducibility Statement

Every number in this paper is read from a committed result file produced by a single open-source pipeline, so no claim rests on an unrecorded run. Section 2 states every setting at the level needed to judge the method, and the released repository records the remainder needed to rerun it, including package pins, environment constraints, seeds and the stage-by-stage runbook. All experiments run on CPU. The evaluation populations are committed as data files with SHA-256 manifests because the simulator is not seed-deterministic end to end; scoring identical subjects is what makes numbers comparable across machines. The discovered expression discussed in the text is given in closed form (Equation 7), so the estimator can be used without re-running any search. Source code, trained weights, committed banks, and result files will be released publicly.

Appendix A SR implementation

The setting of PySR contains maximum complexity 5050 (node count), argument-complexity caps of 99 on the transcendentals, nesting constraints that forbid log⁡log\log\log, exp⁡exp\exp\exp, and log⁡exp\log\exp, and max⁡(31,3×threads)\max(31,3\times\text{threads}) populations. Everything else stays at PySR defaults. Runs are budgeted by wall clock (12001200 s each).

A.1 The objective-weight sweep

The recovery weight λ\lambda of Equation 5 was swept over five values with the operators, no-constants rule, search budget, test subjects and estimator held fixed. Each value pools 2020 or more independently seeded searches, because the search, not the expression, is the unit of replication. All expressions from one search share that search, and the proportion recovering all four parameters varies from zero to over 60%60\% across searches at the same λ\lambda. Averaged over searches, the rate is 1.5%1.5\% at λ=0\lambda=0 and 18.5%18.5\% at λ=1\lambda=1, with non-overlapping 95%95\% bootstrap intervals, and 1515 of the 2020 searches at λ=1\lambda=1 found at least one expression that recovers all four parameters, against 88 of 3636 at λ=0\lambda=0. The effect of the recovery term therefore does not rest on a few searches. Three searches were run at a time throughout, since a search run with a different number of threads explores differently. The λ=0\lambda=0 row pools two sets of MSE searches with identical settings (operators, no-constants rule, 12001200 s per search, maximum size 5050), 1616 searches on ungrouped training rows and 2020 on the grouped training set shared with the other values of λ\lambda. Both sets of rows were simulated and scored by the same neural likelihood. The searches on the shared set recovered all four parameters less often (33 of 562562, 0.5%0.5\%) than the others (99 of 421421, 2.1%2.1\%), so pooling them, if anything, understates the effect of the recovery term.

Table 3gives the numbers behind Section 4.2. The proportion of expressions recovering all four parameters rises from 1.2%1.2\% at λ=0\lambda=0 to 19.5%19.5\% at λ=1\lambda=1 and falls to 2.1%2.1\% at λ=10\lambda=10, so the recovery term helps only over a range of weights. With the density term negligible, the search likely loses the signal that guides it toward sensible expressions, and the recovery term alone is too coarse to replace it. Two further costs appear at high λ\lambda. The non-decision time tt, which is recovered under almost any structure, drops from 99%99\% to 81%81\%, so a search that stops caring about density fit loses the parameter that was never at risk. The start point zz, the hardest parameter at every weight, is recovered most often at λ=3\lambda=3 rather than at λ=1\lambda=1, so the weight that is best for all four parameters jointly is not the best for each one. Divergent transitions are most frequent in the middle of the range, with a median of 77 per expression at λ=3\lambda=3 against 11 at λ=0\lambda=0.

Appendix B The neural likelihood: architecture, gate, and checks

Training data hygiene.

Simulated trials enter the training bank only if they are finite and 0<RT<200<\mathrm{RT}<20 s (about 299,900299{,}900 of 300,000300{,}000 survive). The classifier’s output probabilities are clipped to [10−6,1−10−6][10^{-6},1{-}10^{-6}] at evaluation. All simulation goes through one entry point wrapping ssm-simulators at package defaults, and the model registry checks its hard-coded parameter ranges against the installed package, so that a breaking upstream change fails loudly instead of silently shifting the prior.

Neural surrogate structure and training details.

The flow is a time-embedded MLP of widths [128,128,128][128,128,128] conditioned on [𝜽,c][\bm{\theta},c], trained by conditional flow matching to learn a velocity field that carries a base density to the target. The classifier is a 2×322\times 32 tanh\tanh network with sigmoid output, trained with a cross-entropy loss. The flow trains with Adam (5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, batch 512512, 5050 epochs) and the classifier with Adam (10−310^{-3}, batch 10241024, 3030 epochs). The classifier is trained first, because the flow-fitting library leaves torch in a no-grad state. A post-training report checks for NaNs, under-training, and overfitting.

Functional check.

Used as the likelihood under NUTS on the 6060 test subjects, the gated neural likelihood recovers the parameters as well as the analytical likelihood does (r=.98r=.98–1.001.00; Figure 2a, second row), so nothing downstream is limited by the neural likelihood.

Appendix C Pipeline data split details

Stage 1.

All data come from committed banks of simulated subjects, each a parameter set 𝜽∼Unif⁡(Θ)\boldsymbol{\theta}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\Theta) with up to 10001000 trials. The banks are shipped as data files with SHA-256 manifests, because the simulator is not seed-deterministic end to end and a re-simulated bank would therefore be different data. The neural likelihood is trained on 15,00015{,}000 parameter sets with 2020 simulated trials each (about 300,000300{,}000 trials), split 75/25 into training and validation.

Stage 2.

The symbolic regression training set scores simulated upper-boundary trials with the neural likelihood, with rows 𝐱i=(𝜽i,RTi)\mathbf{x}_{i}=(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\mathrm{RT}_{i}) and targets log⁡pϕ​(RTi,c=1∣𝜽i)\log p_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\mathrm{RT}_{i},c{=}1\mid\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}). It is organized as G=800G=800 parameter sets 𝜽(g)\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(g)}, g=1,…,Gg=1,\dots,G, with K=20K=20 trials each (16,00016{,}000 rows in total). The grouping is essential, because several RT\mathrm{RT} draws at a fixed 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} are what make the recovery proxy of Equation 6 computable. The proxy uses a precomputed block of P⋅G⋅M⋅K=4⋅50⋅9⋅5=9,000P\cdot G\cdot M\cdot K=4\cdot 50\cdot 9\cdot 5=9{,}000 rows (G=50G=50 parameter sets, M=9M=9 grid values per parameter, and K=5K=5 trials), appended to the training array once.

Stages 3–4.

Two further disjoint banks of simulated subjects, with 10001000 trials per subject, are used for scoring. Every candidate expression is scored with NUTS on 6060 test subjects, which are used both to rank the expressions and to report their recovery in Section 4. A further 9090 subjects from the same bank were used by no step of the pipeline and serve only as the held-out check of Section H.2. The faster posterior-mode screen of Appendix D uses 4040 separate subjects.

Appendix D The screen agrees on every marginal and disagrees on the winners

The posterior-mode screen and the full posterior (NUTS) agree closely on marginals. On the λ=1\lambda=1 searches, the mean number of parameters passed is 2.522.52 against 2.592.59, the number passed per expression correlates at .80.80 between the two, and it is identical for 71%71\% of expressions. That agreement is what makes a cheap screen look trustworthy, until one asks which expressions it picks. The screen passes 104104 expressions and the full posterior passes 9595, but only 7373 are shared, so a screen-gated pipeline would have promoted 3131 expressions the full posterior rejects and discarded 2222 of the 9595 that recover. The screen also exaggerates the effect of the objective. It puts the gain from λ=0\lambda=0 to λ=1\lambda=1 at about 4141-fold (0.5%→21.4%0.5\%\to 21.4\%), where the full posterior puts it at about 1616-fold (1.2%→19.5%1.2\%\to 19.5\%). The mode fit is the same kind of object as the recovery proxy the search optimized, so part of the screen-level gain is the screen rewarding the search’s own shortcut. A cheap proxy that shares structure with the search loss cannot also be the judge.

Appendix E The applied case: hierarchical DDM on Cavanagh

Full model.

Every parameter varies by participant. Each of vv, aa, zz and tt has its own group mean and spread, non-centred and mapped through a sigmoid onto the simulator’s range, so that draws stay in the region the expressions were validated on without a clip that would remove the gradient. The upper bound on tt is set per participant at that participant’s fastest trial. Drift rate also carries the frontal-theta covariate as a single population slope, as in the original analysis. The 100100 expressions are the best of those that recover all four parameters, ranked by their weakest correlation. Of these, 9696 converged (R^<1.01\widehat{R}<1.01), at a median of 7373 s each, against 174174 s for the analytical likelihood under the same model and sampler settings.

Across the 9696, the between-participant spread relative to the analytical likelihood is a median of 0.580.58 for vv (inflated in 36%36\% of expressions), 0.810.81 for aa, 1.011.01 for tt and 1.831.83 for zz, and rank agreement with the analytical likelihood is .93.93, .97.97, .90.90 and .29.29, respectively. Thus aa and tt are ordered correctly at the participant level, and vv is ordered correctly but compressed in spread. The expressions also estimated non-decision time a median of 5959 ms later than the analytical likelihood did. Because the expressions are unnormalized, part of these group-level differences may come from the missing 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}-dependent normalizer rather than from the fit to the data. The start point zz is ranked poorly (median .29.29, 1010th percentile −0.13-0.13), but the participants barely differ on it. Their analytical posterior means span only .48.48 to .50.50, and even the neural likelihood agrees with the analytical ranking at only .72.72, so the ranking is dominated by small approximation errors rather than by a failure specific to the closed forms.

Simpler model for timing.

To time a larger set of expressions under a common model, we also fit a model in which only the drift rate varies by participant. Drift has a population intercept (𝒩⁡(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1) prior), a frontal-theta slope (𝒩⁡(0,0.5)\mathcal{N}(0,0.5)), and a non-centred participant offset whose spread has a half-normal prior with scale 0.50.5. The parameters a∼Unif⁡(0.3,2.5)a\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0.3,2.5), z∼Unif⁡(0.1,0.9)z\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0.1,0.9) and t∼Unif⁡(0,tmax)t\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,t_{\max}) are shared across participants, with tmaxt_{\max} just below the fastest response in the dataset. We fit this model with the analytical likelihood and with each of 267267 expressions that recover all four parameters, using 10001000 warm-up and 10001000 sampling iterations in four chains on one core. Of the expressions, 213213 converged. The analytical likelihood and a representative expression needed about the same number of gradient evaluations (108,392108{,}392 and 100,184100{,}184), so the speed-up reflects the cost of each evaluation inside the fitted model (3.73.7 against 0.130.13 ms). Most expressions (163163 of the 213213 that converged) placed the shared non-decision time at its upper bound, the fastest response in the dataset. Among the 5050 that did not, the median fit was faster still (1111 s), so the speed-up does not depend on these fits.

Appendix F Calibration and verification procedure

Recovery across a population does not guarantee that an expression describes any individual subject well. We therefore ran two further checks on the validated expressions, each against a control that makes its number interpretable. The posterior predictive check follows standard workflow tooling (Fengler et al., 2026). We fit 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} with the expression as the likelihood, push each posterior draw through the simulator, and compare the result with the observed trials by the KS distance on choice-signed RTs. We judge it not against the predictive at the true 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, a ceiling that no estimator with finite error attains, but against an unbiased estimator perturbed to have the same recovery. Simulation-based calibration (Talts et al., 2018) is run on data generated from the expression itself, with exp⁡f\exp f normalized on a fixed grid. It therefore tests the sampler, the compiled expression and the normalization together, so any miscalibration on simulated data would be attributable to the estimator rather than to this machinery. The analytical likelihood is run through both checks unchanged as a control.

They come from two searches, with Expressions 1, 2 and 5 from one search at λ=3\lambda=3 and Expressions 3 and 4 from one at λ=1\lambda=1, so they are variations on a shared structure rather than five independent discoveries. Appendix H DDM setting details and supplementary analyses

H.1 Setting details

Θ=[−3,3]×[0.3,2.5]×[0.1,0.9]×[0,2]\Theta=[-3,3]\times[0.3,2.5]\times[0.1,0.9]\times[0,2] is the simulator’s own, and serves as the simulation range, prior support, and reference for the bounds check throughout. Reflecting about zero gives an exact symmetry,

p⁡(RT,c=−1∣𝜽)=p⁡(RT,c=+1∣ς⁡(𝜽)),ς⁡(v,a,z,t)=(−v,a, 1−z,t),p(\mathrm{RT},c{=}-1\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})=p(\mathrm{RT},c{=}+1\mid\varsigma(\boldsymbol{\theta})),\qquad\varsigma(v,a,z,t)=(-v,\,a,\,1{-}z,\,t), (8)

so we model only the upper boundary and evaluate a lower-boundary trial at ς⁡(𝜽)\varsigma(\boldsymbol{\theta}). The Navarro–Fuss series (Navarro & Fuss, 2009) is used only as a reference for measuring ceilings, never as a regression target, because the method is meant for models that have no such formula.

H.2 Supplementary analyses

Two choices in the recovery objective.

Both were validated against 422422 NUTS-scored expressions. The aggregation in Equation 5 is a mean over parameters rather than a minimum, because a minimum over four noisy estimates amplifies noise. And the correlation term is kept even though the edge term alone scored slightly better on the pools then available. An argmax away from the grid edge can be achieved by interior optima that track nothing, and a search optimizing that statistic directly would hunt for exactly that kind of shortcut.

Sampler settings do not change verdicts.

Refitting the two symbolic expressions of Figure 2a on 3030 test subjects with 20002000 warm-up and 20002000 sampling iterations in 44 chains, instead of the standard 500500 and 500500 in 22 chains, moves recovery by at most .04.04 and never reverses which objective wins. The recovery-objective expression goes from .880/.872/.897/.984.880/.872/.897/.984 to .917/.874/.901/.984.917/.874/.901/.984 for v/a/z/tv/a/z/t, the MSE expression from .855/.843/.722/.978.855/.843/.722/.978 to .853/.844/.697/.978.853/.844/.697/.978, and the median per-subject R^\widehat{R} improves from 1.0051.005 to 1.0011.001. A broader re-verification refit 473473 expressions drawn from all five values of λ\lambda, selected as near the criterion (267267), in the worst decile of divergent transitions (157157), or in the worst decile of R^\widehat{R} (159159), and the groups overlap. Of these, 1212 gained a pass, 33 lost one, and 458458 were unchanged, with a median shift in the weakest correlation of −0.0001-0.0001 and 90%90\% of shifts within [−.066,+.057][-.066,+.057]. Eleven of the 1212 gains were in the near-criterion group, so the standard settings were not distorting verdicts.

Held-out subjects.

The 6060 test subjects were used both to rank the expressions and to report their recovery, so the top five could be favored by chance. The same simulated bank holds 9090 further subjects that no step of the pipeline used. We refit the top five on these subjects, together with the known leading-term form and the MSE expression of Figure 2, using 20002000 warm-up and 20002000 sampling iterations in 44 chains (Table 4). All five expressions still recover every parameter. Their weakest correlation falls by a median of .02.02 from the ranking subjects, the same as for the known form, which was never selected, so most of the change reflects the new subjects rather than the selection. The exceptions are Expressions 3 and 4, which fall by .07.07 and .03.03 and come from the same search. The longer sampling moves no correlation of the five by more than .05.05 relative to the standard settings, but it does not resolve convergence for every subject. For Expressions 1, 3 and 4, R^\widehat{R} stays above 1.011.01 for 2525 to 3636 of the 9090 subjects, whereas Expression 5 converges for all of them and Expression 2 for all but 66. Expression 2 has the most divergent transitions (33033303, about 0.5%0.5\% of draws).

Simulation-based calibration.

With exp⁡f\exp f normalized on a fixed log-spaced grid (grid and adaptive quadrature agree to within 1.6×10−51.6\times 10^{-5} in log⁡Z\log Z) and data generated from the expression itself, SBC rank statistics (Talts et al., 2018) pass for all five expressions of Table 1 (Figure 7). Over 200200 simulations of 10001000 trials, rank dispersion for v/a/z/tv/a/z/t is 1.02/1.01/0.95/1.011.02/1.01/0.95/1.01, 0.98/0.98/1.04/0.920.98/0.98/1.04/0.92, 1.02/0.97/1.06/1.011.02/0.97/1.06/1.01, 0.95/1.09/1.01/0.920.95/1.09/1.01/0.92 and 1.03/1.00/0.96/0.991.03/1.00/0.96/0.99 for Expressions 1–5, against 0.92/0.90/1.01/0.950.92/0.90/1.01/0.95 for the analytical likelihood run through the same procedure. Nineteen of the twenty combinations sit inside the 95%95\% simultaneous band, and the analytical likelihood is outside on one of its own four. The sampler, the compiled expression and the normalization are therefore validated together. The scope of this check should be stated precisely. Because the data are generated from the same normalized density that serves as the likelihood, a failure would indict the machinery rather than the model. The check does not cover the unnormalized ff used in the pipeline, which differs from the normalized density by a 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}-dependent term.

Do the recovered parameters reproduce behavior?

Against the predictive at the true 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, the expressions fit worse (median KS .130.130 against .036.036 for Expression 2), but that reference is a ceiling no estimator with finite error attains, so the comparison only restates that recovery is imperfect. Against a fair null, an unbiased estimator perturbed to the expression’s own recovery rr, Expression 2 does better (.130.130 against .156.156; Figure 8), as do three of the other four expressions, while the MSE expression reaches only .287.287 on the same subjects. The predictive misfit of the recovery-objective expressions is therefore no larger than their recovery level implies, and the objective improves predictive quality as well as recovery.

Population-level estimator audit.

For each expression, we computed its population argmax 𝜽∗(𝜽)=argmaxϑ𝔼p(⋅∣𝜽)f(ϑ,⋅)\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\operatorname*{argmax}_{\vartheta}\mathbb{E}_{p(\cdot\mid\boldsymbol{\theta})}f(\vartheta,\cdot) by quadrature against the analytical density, which is the value its estimates converge to with unlimited trials. This shows that 10001000 trials is already effectively asymptotic. The recovery implied by 𝜽∗\boldsymbol{\theta}^{*} reproduces the measured NUTS rr with median gaps of 0.0000.000 to +0.022+0.022 (correlations .75.75–.95.95 per parameter), so the pass rates of Table 3 are limited by the structure of the expressions rather than by noise. The same audit locates the zz bottleneck. Among the 487487 expressions scored at λ=1\lambda=1 (the 486486 of Table 3 plus a reference closed form), the limit for zz clears the criterion for 141141 (29%29\%, close to the measured 25.1%25.1\%), against 399399 for vv and 479479 for tt. The reference closed form, the logarithm of the leading term of the small-time series (Navarro & Fuss, 2009), is exponential-family separable in u=RT−tu=\mathrm{RT}-t, with sufficient statistic T⁡(u)=(∑u,∑1/u)T(u)=(\sum u,\sum 1/u) and log⁡u\log u base measure, and tt enters only through the support. That role of tt is also the source of fragility. Because tt is effectively estimated from the sample minimum, fast-guess contamination (replacing trials, with nn fixed) reduces the number of the 9696 expressions at λ=1\lambda=1 that recover all four parameters (including the reference form) from 8181 to 5353, 2929, 22 and 00 at 00, 0.250.25, 0.50.5, 11 and 2%2\% contamination. This is a breakdown point of order 1/n1/n, as expected for a parameter estimated from the sample minimum.

Appendix I AI use statement

In this work, we used generative AI tools (Claude, Anthropic, through Claude Code) to generate the initial scaffold of the pipeline code. We have not used generative AI tools to propose the research question or the recovery-directed objective, or to interpret results, and generating synthetic data sets, formulating mathematical claims, writing proofs, translation and qualitative data analysis are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to help write and organize the results and the appendix. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. All code was verified by the authors, and every number in the paper was checked against the result files the code produced. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.
